sections.heading: Retail plus wholesale colocation on one campus
bullets: Retail colocation rents cabinets and cages to many customers; wholesale leases whole halls or buildings to a few giants. Most operators pick a lane — Switch runs both on the same campuses, which is why its securitized pool shows 550+ customers while its AI halls host single hyperscale tenants

A mixed tenant base changes the risk math: hundreds of sticky enterprise contracts smooth revenue, while a handful of AI leases drive growth — rating agencies price the blend (~84% of Switch trust revenue is from investment-grade tenants)

The 'operator-landlord' model: the landlord owns land, shell, power and cooling and staffs operations 24/7; tenants own the IT gear. Rent is typically take-or-pay on reserved capacity — contractual cash flow that can be financed like infrastructure
Campus-scale matters because power, security, staff and fiber amortize over more megawatts — one reason operators brand giant single-market 'campuses' instead of scattering small sites

sections.heading: Availability ratings: Uptime Tiers I-IV — and what a self-declared 'Tier 5' is
bullets: The Uptime Institute's Tier system is the industry's availability ladder: Tier I (basic), Tier II (redundant components), Tier III (concurrently maintainable — any part serviceable without downtime), Tier IV (fault-tolerant — survives any single equipment failure, ~96-hour on-site power ride-through expectation)

'Tier 5 Platinum' is Switch's own standard, not an Uptime rating — no third party audits or certifies it. Honest reading: it is a marketing-plus-engineering superset that bundles real design choices (100-hour standby power vs Tier IV's 12-hour benchmark as Switch frames it, zero roof penetrations, indefinite waterless cooling, 10 on-net carriers, per-rack security) with brand control

Why operators self-declare: certification constrains design and hands the brand to the certifier. Why buyers should still ask questions: a self-declared standard can change definitions, and no independent body verifies compliance

The useful skill: translate any vendor tier claim back into the four questions that matter — can it ride through grid loss (how long?), can every component be maintained live, what breaks concurrently, and who verified it

sections.heading: Heat containment: hot aisles, T-SCIF and keeping water out of the hall
bullets: Basic physics: servers pull in cool air and exhaust hot air. If hot exhaust mixes back into intakes, chillers work overtime — so modern halls separate the streams. Hot-aisle containment walls off the exhaust side and ducts it away; cold air floods the room

Switch's patented T-SCIF (Thermal Separate Compartment in Facility) is containment taken to its logical end: racks sit in enclosed thermal rows where 100% of exhaust is captured into an overhead hot plenum and returned to cooling units — the IT floor never sees mixed air

Its multi-mode exterior cooling units (TSC series) sit outside the building shell and switch between cooling methods (direct evaporative, indirect, DX refrigeration) as weather changes — desert-optimized, and it keeps all cooling water outside the data hall, which is both a leak-risk and a security argument

Same idea, new scale: the EVO 'chamber' encloses AI racks in their own environment with five separate liquid loops at independent pressures/temperatures — containment logic applied to liquid cooling, designed for racks that air physically cannot cool

sections.heading: The density ladder: why 20kW racks became 2MW design targets
bullets: An enterprise rack draws 5-15kW and air cooling suffices. GPU training racks (NVIDIA GB200/GB300 NVL72 class) draw ~130-150kW — beyond air's practical limit, so coolant must touch the chips via cold plates fed from coolant distribution units (CDUs)

Vendors now design for what's next, not what ships: Switch's EVO rating of 'up to 2MW per rack' anticipates late-decade rack-scale systems. Design ratings are ceilings, not deployed reality — a key skill is distinguishing 'rated for' from 'operating at'

Why density keeps climbing: AI training profits from shorter copper interconnects — packing more compute per rack cuts network latency and cost, so the industry consolidates whole rows into single mega-racks

Hybrid cooling is the transition state: liquid-to-chip for the silicon plus air handling for everything else (power supplies, storage, people). A hall that can serve any mix future-proofs the landlord against tenant hardware churn

A digital-twin 'facility operating system' (Switch's LDC EVO on NVIDIA Omniverse) simulates thermal and electrical behavior before hardware lands — at 2MW per rack, commissioning by trial-and-error is no longer survivable

sections.heading: 100% renewable: what the claim mechanically means
bullets: Three procurement tools: (1) PPAs — long-term contracts to buy a specific plant's output, which can finance new construction ('additionality'); (2) RECs — certificates representing 1MWh of renewable generation bought separately from the power itself; (3) utility green tariffs — the utility bundles renewable supply into your rate

'100% renewable since 2016' claims (Switch's, and most of the industry's) are annual-matching claims: total renewable MWh bought ≥ total MWh consumed over a year. The electrons at 3am are still whatever the grid is burning — which is why 24/7 hourly matching is the emerging gold standard

Additionality is the quality test: buying RECs from a 20-year-old hydro dam changes nothing; contracting a new-build plant adds clean supply. Switch's own Tier 5 standard requires renewables from 'new local projects' — the stronger form of the claim

Firm vs variable renewables: solar and wind are cheap but intermittent; geothermal runs 24/7. A 20-year, 13MW geothermal PPA is small in MW but strategically different in kind — it buys always-on carbon-free supply that matches a data center's flat load

sections.heading: Campus-scale power procurement: queues, LCs and paying your own way
bullets: Getting hundreds of new megawatts means the utility must build substations and transmission first — and interconnection queues for large loads run years. The scarce asset in this industry is approved megawatts with a delivery date, not land

Utilities demand performance assurance before building: if the data center walks away, ratepayers would eat the stranded infrastructure. Letters of credit (a bank's promise to pay if the customer defaults) are how developers collateralize those promises — Switch raised a first-of-kind $2.6B (later $3.5B) syndicated LC facility precisely for this

The ratepayer-politics layer: when data centers strain grids, household bills rise and backlash follows (state audits, moratoria, referenda). The industry's pre-emptive answer is 'pay your own way' — developer-funded infrastructure, dedicated rate classes, self-supplied water — now formalized in state-level standards like Texas's

Nevada context: Switch's home grid (NV Energy) sits outside the big organized markets like ERCOT and PJM — a vertically integrated utility state where large customers negotiate special contracts and can even pay exit fees to buy power on the open market, something Switch historically fought for

sections.heading: Nuclear offtake: what a 12GW 'master power agreement' actually commits
bullets: Small modular / advanced reactors (like Oklo's Aurora, ~15MW-class fast reactors initially) promise factory-built, siteable, always-on carbon-free power — exactly the load profile data centers want — but none of the new designs are operating commercially yet; the first Aurora is targeted for late 2027 at Idaho National Laboratory

A master power agreement is a framework, not a purchase: it sets terms under which many individual, binding PPAs may be signed as projects hit milestones. '12GW through 2044' means an option book that could become hundreds of reactor deployments — or far fewer if licensing, cost or schedule slips

Why sign non-binding gigawatts? The buyer gets queue position and price framing on future firm power at near-zero cost today; the reactor startup gets order-book credibility for fundraising and regulators. Read announcements of this species as strategic options, not supply
The licensing gate: US reactors need NRC approval (combined license applications, multi-year reviews). Any nuclear-powered-data-center timeline is bounded by the regulator, not the construction crew

Scale check: 12GW is roughly ten large nuclear units' worth of capacity — several times Switch's entire announced campus pipeline — which itself signals the agreement is about long-run optionality across decades

sections.heading: Water: zero-water cooling and 'net positive' claims
bullets: Traditional evaporative cooling trades water for electricity: evaporating water removes heat cheaply but consumes millions of gallons. Closed-loop designs circulate the same fluid forever and reject heat through air-cooled equipment — near-zero water at somewhat higher power draw

Desert operators lead on waterless design out of necessity: community water objections can kill permits faster than power constraints in NV/AZ. Switch markets zero-water cooling for servers and GPUs plus recycled-effluent pipeline projects in host communities

'Net positive water' means funding restoration/reuse projects that return more water to the basin than operations consume — a design-plus-offset structure (Switch's stated goal: replenish up to 2x its use over the coming decade)

The metric: WUE (liters of water per kWh of IT energy). Near-zero WUE via closed loops is the emerging expectation for AI-scale campuses; when evaluating claims, ask whether the figure covers the power plant's water too (source WUE) or just the site

sections.heading: Financing the machine: ABS, CMBS and the private-to-public round trip
bullets: Data-center securitization pools lease cash flows from stabilized, tenant-filled buildings into rated notes: ABS (master-trust structures secured by the tenant leases and assets, expandable with new series) vs CMBS (mortgage bonds against specific properties — Switch's $2.4B deal was 'single-asset single-borrower'). Both let a private company borrow at investment-grade-like pricing without public equity

Tranching splits one cash-flow pool by seniority: AAA seniors get paid first at low yield; BBB/BB juniors absorb losses first for higher yield. Green-bond designation (verified use of proceeds for sustainable assets) widens the buyer base

The take-private playbook in one line: buy with bank debt ($11B, 2022) → refinance the expensive acquisition debt with securitizations as assets stabilize (retired 100% by mid-2025) → shift issuance to funding new construction → relist at an AI-cycle multiple (reported $40-80B range) — the securitization market effectively financed the equity markup

Why the trust disclosures matter to an analyst: a private company reveals nothing quarterly, but every rated ABS forces disclosure of collateral (buildings, MW, customer counts, credit mix) — read the rating reports as a proxy income statement

sections.heading: The patent-moat strategy vs the land-bank strategy
bullets: Two ways to defend a data-center franchise: control scarce inputs (land + interconnection queues — the Vantage/QTS model) or control design IP and brand (patents + proprietary standards — the Switch model). Most operators blend both; Switch is the extreme IP case with 950+ issued and pending patent claims held around its founder's designs

Founder-designer concentration cuts both ways: coherent product vision and fast iteration (one authority signs off), but key-person risk that public-market investors will price — the S-1 risk-factors section for a founder-designed platform is worth reading closely

Patents in this industry protect containment structures, cooling units, power distribution ('POWER SPINE') and roof systems ('Switch SHIELD') — mechanical/architectural IP with long lives, unlike fast-cycling IT hardware

The test of a design moat is external validation: world-first NVIDIA GB200/GB300 bring-ups landing in Switch halls (via CoreWeave/Dell) is the strongest public evidence its density designs work at the frontier — stronger than any self-published spec

sections.heading: The competitive map: where Switch sits
bullets: Wholesale pure-plays (Vantage, Aligned, STACK, CloudHQ, QTS): compete on giga-scale build-to-suit and time-to-power; Vantage is even a DigitalBridge sibling — same sponsor, different product philosophy (standardized blueprint at scale vs patented density flagship)

Retail/interconnection REITs (Equinix, Digital Realty): public giants whose moat is network ecosystems and global reach; Switch counters with campus power depth, Tier 5 branding and the telecom cooperative, not network density

Energy-first entrants (Crusoe; miner-pivots like Applied Digital, TeraWulf, Core Scientific): bring power positions and speed, but thin operating track records with enterprise tenants — Switch's 26-year uptime story and IG-heavy tenant base is the counter-pitch
Neoclouds (CoreWeave, Lambda) are tenants more than rivals — they rent the halls and buy the GPUs; landlords hosting their flagship deployments convert that into marketing

Switch's distinctive bundle: self-authored standard + patent estate + retail-and-wholesale mix + AI-factory product + renewable-since-2016 record — no single peer holds all five; the open question is whether that bundle scales as fast as the land-bank giants build

flashcards.q: Uptime Tier III vs Tier IV — what capability separates them?
flashcards.a: Tier III is concurrently maintainable: any component can be serviced without downtime. Tier IV is fault-tolerant: the facility rides through any single unplanned equipment failure, not just planned maintenance.

flashcards.q: What is 'Tier 5 Platinum' — and what's the honest caveat?
flashcards.a: Switch's own facility standard: a superset of Tier IV-style redundancy plus 30+ extra requirements (100-hour standby power, waterless cooling operation, 10 on-net carriers, zero roof penetrations, mandatory renewables, PUE < 1.3). Caveat: it is self-declared and marketing-controlled — no independent body like the Uptime Institute audits or certifies it.

flashcards.q: Why does hot-aisle containment save energy?
flashcards.a: It stops hot server exhaust from mixing back into cold intake air. Cooling systems then work against a clean temperature difference instead of a blended room, so chillers run less for the same IT load.

flashcards.q: What does Switch's T-SCIF design do conceptually?
flashcards.a: It encloses racks in a separate thermal compartment: 100% of hot exhaust is captured into an overhead plenum and returned to cooling units outside the hall, so supply and return air never mix on the IT floor.

flashcards.q: Why must a 130kW+ GPU rack be liquid-cooled?
flashcards.a: Air physically cannot carry heat away fast enough at that density — the required airflow and temperature difference become impossible. Coolant must contact the chips via cold plates, fed through coolant distribution units (CDUs).

flashcards.q: A vendor rates halls for 'up to 2MW per rack' while today's biggest racks draw ~150kW. How do you read that?
flashcards.a: As design headroom, not deployed reality. It claims the power delivery and liquid loops can scale to future rack-scale systems without rebuilding — check what's actually operating before treating it as a spec.

flashcards.q: PPA vs REC — what's the difference and which drives new clean supply?
flashcards.a: A PPA is a long-term contract for a specific plant's output — it can finance new construction (additionality). A REC is a certificate for 1MWh of renewable generation bought separately from the power. PPAs for new-build plants change the grid; loose RECs mostly change accounting.

flashcards.q: What does '100% renewable since 2016' typically mean mechanically?
flashcards.a: Annual matching: renewable MWh purchased ≥ MWh consumed over the year. It does not mean every hour runs on clean electrons — that stronger claim is 24/7 hourly matching, which almost no one achieves yet.

flashcards.q: Why is a small 13MW geothermal PPA strategically interesting for a data-center operator?
flashcards.a: Geothermal is firm, 24/7 carbon-free power that matches a data center's flat load — unlike variable solar/wind. It adds always-on clean supply, upgrading the quality (not just the quantity) of a renewable portfolio.

flashcards.q: What is a performance letter of credit, and why do utilities demand them from data-center developers?
flashcards.a: A bank guarantee that pays the utility if the customer abandons its commitments. Utilities must build substations and transmission before the load arrives; the LC protects ratepayers from stranded costs — which is why multi-GW developers now raise billion-scale syndicated LC facilities.

flashcards.q: What does a non-binding 12GW nuclear 'master power agreement' actually commit?
flashcards.a: A framework only: terms under which individual, binding PPAs may be signed as reactor projects hit milestones. It grants queue position and price framing to the buyer and order-book credibility to the reactor company — but zero megawatts are guaranteed until each PPA binds.

flashcards.q: What gates the timeline of any US advanced-reactor deployment?
flashcards.a: NRC licensing — combined license applications and multi-year safety reviews. Construction is fast by comparison; the regulator, not the crew, sets the critical path.

flashcards.q: How does closed-loop cooling achieve near-zero water use, and what's the trade?
flashcards.a: The same fluid circulates forever, rejecting heat through air-cooled equipment instead of evaporating water away. The trade: somewhat higher electricity use — you swap WUE for a bit of PUE.

flashcards.q: ABS vs single-asset CMBS in data-center finance?
flashcards.a: ABS: a master trust secured by lease cash flows and assets, expandable with new note series as the fleet grows. SASB CMBS: a mortgage bond against specific named properties. Both convert private buildings into rated, investment-grade-priced debt.

flashcards.q: Why do ABS rating disclosures matter for analyzing a private data-center company?
flashcards.a: They force public collateral disclosure — building counts, square footage, MW, customer counts, tenant credit mix — creating a proxy income statement for a company that otherwise reports nothing.

flashcards.q: Walk the take-private-to-IPO financing playbook in four steps.
flashcards.a: (1) Acquire with bank debt; (2) refinance the expensive acquisition debt via ABS/CMBS as assets stabilize; (3) redirect securitization to fund new construction once the LBO debt is retired; (4) relist at the new cycle's multiple. The credit markets finance the equity markup.

flashcards.q: Patent-moat vs land-bank strategy in the data-center industry?
flashcards.a: Land-bank: control scarce sites and interconnection queue positions — value in approved megawatts. Patent-moat: control facility design IP and a branded standard — value in what you can build and charge for anywhere. Land constrains rivals; IP differentiates product.

flashcards.q: What is a facility 'digital twin' operating system and why does AI density make it necessary?
flashcards.a: A physics-accurate live 3D model of the facility (thermal, electrical, telemetry) used to simulate changes before touching hardware. At hundreds of kW per rack, a cooling misstep destroys equipment in seconds — commissioning and operating by simulation replaces trial-and-error DCIM.
